title: Preserving AI Systems for Auditability and Reproducibility: A Preservation Framework and an Evidence Map of 185 Sources
content: An organization may have to explain an AI-assisted decision years after it was made. The evidence it needs is described across archival guidance, regulation, standards and research, but no source in this review brings those four views together. This scoping review extracted 1,519 requirement statements from 185 sources (10 guidance documents, 17 regulatory texts, 23 standards, 135 research papers) and coded each against the AI System Preservation Matrix: seven system components by four capabilities (intact bits, loadable, behavior within a stated tolerance, decision context). Two coding passes, the second blind to the first, agreed at Cohen's kappa 0.87 to 0.95 per family. Of the statements, 94.5% include a retention requirement (L1) and 9.2% include a requirement to reproduce or test behavior (L3); the categories may overlap. Another 43% concern training data, evaluation or risk documentation rather than the system in use. In four of the 28 cells no guidance, regulation or standard asks for re-runnable prompts, for loadable or re-runnable retrieval stores, or for re-runnable agent tools and state; only research proposals do, and broader readings of the definitions find only monitoring and identification requirements there. Archival guidance leaves 13 cells empty, including every agent cell. I use the map to propose a three-tier preservation framework: a minimum evidence floor, recommended capabilities and proposals for gaps not covered by the reviewed normative sources. A desk check on three reference configurations supports it; it is not yet validated in operation. The matrix, a machine-readable profile, the evidence table, a rebuild script and a worked evidence package are released as data, with nine recommendations naming who can close which gap.
